title: What Rectify is
text: Rectify Mirror a connected device, drag a box over the bug, and hand Claude Code a payload it can actually act on — the frame, per-annotation crops, the view hierarchy and a generated prompt. Then re-capture the device and let Rectify prove, per annotation, that the fix landed. Get started The loop Every other tool in this space does one leg of it. Rectify's whole claim is the round trip. Mirror A live frame from an Android handset or emulator over adb , or an iOS simulator over xcrun simctl and idb . Annotate Drag on the frame. The exact pixels freeze, and the box becomes a numbered annotation with a comment field. Measure Hold ⌥ and the box snaps to the matched hierarchy node, reporting dp gaps to its neighbours. Send One action packages frame, crops, hierarchy XML and prompt, and publishes them for the local MCP server to serve. Verify Re-capture the device and diff each annotated region against the frozen original. Matches resolve; mismatches offer a one-click re-send. Why it exists Spotting a visual bug on a real device is easy. Describing it precisely is not. The usual path is a screenshot, a sentence of prose about roughly where the problem is, and the loss of everything that made the observation useful — the exact region, the pixel or dp gap, the view that owns it. Then, once the agent claims a fix, there is no way to check it other than re-opening the app and eyeballing the same spot from memory. Rectify keeps that context attached to the report, and keeps the original frame around so the check is a diff rather than a recollection. What it is not Not a cloud servic

title: Installation
text: Installation Rectify is not published as a binary yet. You build it from source, which takes one Gradle command, and you wire its MCP server into Claude Code, which takes one JSON entry. Requirements Host macOS. The device tooling below is macOS-first, and packaging targets the OS you build on. JDK 21 or newer. Android devices adb on your PATH , or an Android SDK at $ANDROID_HOME / $ANDROID_SDK_ROOT . iOS simulators Xcode command line tools — xcrun and simctl . idb as well if you want physical devices. You need neither toolchain to launch Rectify. It detects what is present and reports the rest as a recoverable error card rather than refusing to start. A note on packaging. ./gradlew packageDmg currently fails on a Homebrew-installed JDK — the Compose plugin blocks it because such builds produce broken bundles. Use a distribution such as Amazon Corretto if you want an installer. Running from Gradle is unaffected. Run it git clone https://github.com/andrew-malitchuk/rectify-kmp.git cd rectify-kmp ./gradlew :desktop-application:run The window opens at 1240×820 and starts polling for devices immediately. Wire up the MCP server Rectify writes each sent batch to a handoff slot on disk. A separate, very small server process reads that slot back out and answers Claude Code over stdio. Claude Code starts and stops that process itself — you never run it by hand. Build the launcher first. There is no packaged distribution, so the binary has to exist before Claude Code can spawn it: ./gradlew :mcp-application:installDist That produces mcp-application/build/install/rectify-mcp/bin/recti

title: Connecting a device
text: Connecting a device Rectify polls for devices every two seconds and shows whatever it finds. There is no connect step to remember — plug something in and it appears. The platform switch The toolbar's leftmost control chooses which world you are looking at: Android or iOS . Each platform has its own discovery loop, its own tool, and its own device list. Switching platforms is a clean break. The previous platform's poll is cancelled, its device list is cleared, and any device you had selected is forgotten — a Pixel is not a thing the iOS tab can mirror, so leaving it named in the toolbar would be a lie. Platform Tool What it finds Android adb devices -l Physical handsets and running emulators Android emulator -list-avds Shut-down AVDs, offered with an inline Boot button iOS xcrun simctl list devices available Simulators, booted or not iOS idb list-targets Physical devices, if idb is installed The picker With a platform selected and something attached, the stage shows Choose what to mirror : Physical device — handsets and iPhones. Virtual devices — emulators and simulators. A shut-down one is still listed, with a Boot button beside it, so you do not have to leave Rectify to start it. Navigate with ↑ ↓ and commit with ↵ , or click. The Start mirroring button does the same thing as ↵ . Esc closes the picker — but only once you have something to go back to. Before your first selection there is nothing behind it, so Esc deliberately does nothing rather than stranding you on an empty stage. Once a device is selected, the toolbar chip shows its name and serial. Click the chip to reo

title: Annotating a frame
text: Annotating a frame Drag to freeze Click and drag anywhere on the live mirror. While you drag you get a dashed red outline, a live size readout in device pixels, and ruler guides along the edges so you can line the box up against something real. Releasing the drag freezes the frame. The exact pixels under your box at that instant become the frozen frame, and the box becomes annotation number 1. Freezing is a render decision, not a transport one. The capture loop keeps running behind the frozen frame, which is why Resume live costs nothing — there is no reconnection to pay for. Write the comment Each annotation gets a popover with a numbered badge matching its box, an autofocused comment field, a size and position line, and a delete control. ↵ saves the comment. Esc dismisses the popover, keeping the annotation. The delete control removes the annotation entirely. The placeholder asks What's wrong here? because that is the question the payload is answering. A comment is optional — an annotation with none is still a region the agent can look at — but a sentence of intent is usually worth more than the crop. More than one Keep dragging. Everything outside the annotation boxes dims, so the frozen frame reads as a set of marked regions rather than a screenshot with boxes on it. When popovers would overlap each other, they relocate to a gutter beside the frame and connect back to their boxes with leader lines, rather than stacking on top of each other over the content you are trying to describe. The toolbar's staged counter tracks how many you have. Clear removes all of them at onc

title: Measure mode
text: Measure mode A box says this region is wrong . Measure mode says by how much, against what . Holding Option Hold ⌥ with the pointer over an annotation box on a frozen frame. Rectify matches the box against the view hierarchy it dumped from the device, snaps to the node underneath, and switches the stage into measuring: The matched node is outlined precisely, replacing your rough drag with the view's real bounds. Neighbouring views get dashed guide boxes. A floating Measuring panel reports the gaps between them, in dp and device pixels. Misalignment is called out in red. Release ⌥ and the stage returns to normal. What gets attached The measurement is written into that annotation's note, prefixed with the ⌥ symbol so it is distinguishable from what you typed: ⌥ item_price 48×17dp That line travels with the payload. The agent receives the gap is 4dp where the sibling is 8dp rather than this looks too close to the thing above it . Why dp and not just pixels A pixel measurement is only meaningful alongside the density it was taken at, and the density is a property of the device, not of the screenshot. Rectify reads it from the hierarchy dump and converts, so the number means the same thing on a 420 dpi handset as on a 560 dpi one — which is the number a layout fix is actually expressed in. When the hierarchy is missing Measure mode needs a hierarchy dump. If the dump failed — the device disconnected, the dump timed out, the app under test blocks it — the status line says so, and ⌥ does nothing rather than snapping to stale coordinates from a previous frame. title: Sending to Claude Code
text: Sending to Claude Code Resolve and Send The toolbar's primary action, or ⌘↵ . It is disabled while nothing is staged and while a send is already in flight. The status line reports each step as it happens: ● Streaming › ● Frozen › ● Dumping hierarchy › ● Sent Dumping hierarchy is the slow one — roughly 2.7 seconds on a typical handset — because it shells out to the device and waits for a full view tree. On success a toast confirms what went where, with the session id and an Open session action that copies it. The mirror resumes live and the staged counter returns to zero. What is in the payload Part Detail Frame The full frozen screenshot, at device resolution. Crops One per annotation, with the red outline baked in. Hierarchy The view-hierarchy XML dump taken at freeze time. Prompt Generated text describing each annotation, including any ⌥ measurement. The crops exist because an agent reading a 1080×2400 frame has to find your region in it first. The hierarchy exists because the price label is misaligned is a different instruction from the view with id item_price is misaligned . How the handoff actually works Rectify does not talk to Claude Code. The two never share a process, a socket or a lifetime. Rectify ──writes──▶ ~/.rectify/handoff ◀──reads── rectify-mcp ──stdio──▶ Claude Code Rectify publishes. The batch is written to a slot at ~/.rectify/handoff , plus its bulk bytes under ~/.rectify/history/ . Claude Code spawns the server. rectify-mcp is a separate, deliberately tiny JVM process. Claude Code starts and stops it; you never run it yourself. The server reads the slo

title: Verify and history
text: Verify and history History ⌘3 , or the History tab. Every batch you have ever sent, newest first, grouped by day. Each row carries a thumbnail, the first comment as a title, the note count, the time, a short batch id, and a status chip. History survives restarts — it is a real SQLite database at ~/.rectify/rectify.db , with the frames and crops beside it under ~/.rectify/history/ . Verify Each row has a Verify action. It is not gated on status: nothing in the current version automatically marks a batch fixed, so gating would make the button unreachable exactly when you want it. Verify does four things: Loads the batch back off disk — the original frozen frame and every annotation rectangle. Re-captures the device as it is right now. Diffs each annotation region, comparing pixels against the original and re-reading the view hierarchy for layout changes. Reports a verdict per annotation, not per batch. The stage shows BEFORE and AFTER side by side, each with its annotation rectangles drawn on, so you can see what the verdict is talking about. Reading the verdicts Verdict Means Fixed The region changed in a way consistent with the report. Still off The region is materially unchanged. The result panel sums it up as n of m fixed , and each row shows the measurement that led to the call — top Δ4dp → 4dp , 66×74dp → 66×74dp . A combined pixel and hierarchy diff is used rather than pixels alone because a layout fix can move a view without changing many pixels, and an unrelated content change can alter a great many pixels without touching the bug. Acting on the result Send follow-up

title: Troubleshooting
text: Troubleshooting Rectify reports problems as structured error cards on the stage rather than as dialogs or log lines: an icon, a title, a plain-language body, a copyable command where one would help, a primary and secondary action, and a diagnostic footer showing exactly what was observed. The footer is the part worth reading when the card itself does not match your situation. adb is not on the PATH Rectify probes, in order: the path you chose yourself, $ANDROID_HOME , $ANDROID_SDK_ROOT , ~/Library/Android/sdk , /opt/homebrew/bin , /usr/local/bin , then PATH . PATH alone is not enough, because a GUI application launched from Finder does not inherit the shell PATH your terminal has — which is why the explicit candidate list exists. Fix it by installing the platform tools, or use Locate adb… on the card to point at the binary directly. Your choice is remembered and re-read on every probe, so changing it mid-session takes effect without a restart. No device detected adb answers but sees nothing attached. USB debugging enabled on the handset? Allow tapped on the authorisation prompt? An unauthorised device is attached but unusable, and the card counts it separately. Cable capable of data, not just charge? Restart adb server on the card runs adb kill-server and lets the next poll start it again. This is the single most effective action for a device that was working a minute ago. Multiple devices connected Not an error — an ambiguity. The card lists what it found inline and defaults its primary action to the top one. Pick the one you meant, or use the toolbar chip to open the full

title: Module map
text: Module map Rectify is 22 Gradle modules. The split is strict and the dependency direction never reverses: presentation → domain → data , with a few shared leaves at the bottom. A warning before you read the source "Android" and "iOS" appear everywhere in this codebase as domain concepts, not build targets. Rectify is a desktop application. Every module is a plain kotlin("jvm") module; there is no Kotlin Multiplatform plugin, no commonMain / desktopMain split, no expect / actual , and no Android or iOS target anywhere. Sources are in the classic src/main/kotlin and src/test/kotlin . AdbHostSource , IosHostSource , SimctlDevicesParser , the ANDROID_SOURCE and IOS_SOURCE Koin qualifiers — those are the product . They are how a desktop app talks to phones. They are not evidence of a mobile build. The repository is still named rectify-kmp , which is also why Compose resource accessors generate under rectify_kmp.* . That is a name, not a target. Entry points Module Role desktop-application The runnable one. main() calls initKoin() then runDesktopApp() . Nothing else. compose-application The app composition: the Rectify window, the Koin graph assembly. A library — it has no main() . mcp-application A second, separate process. The MCP server Claude Code spawns over stdio. docs-generator A build-time tool that renders this site out of docs/ . The runnable module is separate from the UI module on purpose: compose-application stays a library so a harness can compose the shell without a process, and desktop-application owns nothing but the entry point and

title: State management
text: State management Feature screens use Orbit MVI . presentation-feature-mirror is the only feature module and therefore the reference shape — match it rather than inventing a variant. Four files Under source/<feature>/ : File Holds XContract.kt XState (UI snapshot, defaults for every field), XSideEffect (one-shot events), XIntent (every user action) XViewModel.kt ContainerHost<XState, XSideEffect> , intent dispatch, all the logic XScreen.kt Resolves the ViewModel from Koin, collects state and side effects XContent.kt Stateless. No Koin, no ViewModel — takes state and emits onIntent The split exists so that everything below XScreen can be rendered from literals. The content layer never resolves a dependency, which is why the whole shell can be previewed and screenshot without a running Koin graph. The shape class MirrorViewModel(/* use cases */) : ContainerHost<MirrorUiState, MirrorSideEffect>, ViewModel() { override val container = container<MirrorUiState, MirrorSideEffect>(MirrorUiState()) { // init-time work only } fun handleIntent(intent: MirrorIntent) = when (intent) { is MirrorIntent.SelectPlatform -> selectPlatform(intent.platform) MirrorIntent.ResolveAndSend -> resolveAndSend() // …exhaustive, no else } private fun selectPlatform(platform: PlatformModel) = intent { reduce { state.copy(platform = platform, /* … */) } } } The when is exhaustive with no else . A new intent that nobody handles is then a compile error rather than a click that silently does nothing. Derived state, not stored state MirrorUiState stores facts and derives presentat

title: Dependency injection
text: Dependency injection Koin, assembled once in compose-application 's initKoin() and started from desktop-application 's main() . The graph public fun initKoin(config: KoinAppDeclaration = {}) { startKoin { config() modules( dataPreferenceImplModule, dataDatabaseImplModule, dataDeviceImplModule, dataRepositoryImplModule, domainUseCaseImplModule, presentationFeatureMirrorModule, ) } } The order reads data → domain → presentation . Koin resolves lazily, so the order is defensive rather than strictly load-bearing — but it documents the dependency direction at the one place where the whole graph is visible, and keeping it is free. Why main() starts it There is no lifecycle callback before main() on the desktop, so the entry point is the only place Koin can be started. initKoin() deliberately does not live inside runDesktopApp() . Bootstrapping DI is the entry point's job, and runDesktopApp() is shared code that a test or a second host could call without wanting a second startKoin . The DI convention plugin dev.rectify.io.convention.di adds Koin dependencies and nothing else — no plugin IDs, no targets. It must be applied alongside library or feature ; on its own the configurations it writes to do not exist yet. koin-core is exposed as api() because consumers need it at compile time to call get() or koinInject() . koin-compose and koin-viewmodel are implementation() — a module that needs them applies the plugin itself. title: Data and persistence
text: Data and persistence Three separate stores, for three different jobs. Preferences data-preference-api defines one generic contract: public interface PreferenceSource<T> { public suspend fun getData(): T public suspend fun setData(data: T) public fun observeData(): Flow<T> } One typed interface per preference ( ThemePreferenceSource : PreferenceSource<ThemePreference> ), one implementation in data-preference-impl . Each holds a MutableStateFlow seeded from the backing store on construction: setData writes through and updates the flow, observeData returns it, and getData re-reads fresh so the first call is correct before anything has subscribed. The backend is multiplatform-settings over java.util.prefs.Preferences , under the node dev.rectify.io . Keys follow pref_<name> and are declared as constants in the implementation. Never change an existing key — it silently orphans the stored value on every existing install. Add a new key and migrate. History — Room data-database-api holds only generic, composable base interfaces: ReadableDataSource<T> , ObservableDataSource<T> , AppendableDataSource<T> , UpsertableDataSource<T> . No entity-specific interface lives there — those are defined where they are consumed, by mixing in whichever bases apply. data-database-impl is the Room implementation: two tables, history_entry (one row per sent batch) and history_annotation (its per-rect children, with FOREIGN KEY … ON DELETE CASCADE , indexed on batchId ). title: Device transport
text: Device transport How a desktop JVM ends up with a bitmap of a phone screen, and a view tree to go with it. One process-spawn site ProcessBuilder appears in exactly one file in the entire repository: data-device-impl/src/main/kotlin/data/device/impl/core/process/ProcessRunner.kt It is internal . Everything that needs to run something routes through it. The audit is one command, and it must print exactly one path: grep -rln "ProcessBuilder" --include="*.kt" . | grep -v /build/ Four details inside it are load-bearing rather than decorative: Two concurrent drains. stdout and stderr are read on separate coroutines. Reading them sequentially deadlocks the moment a large screencap payload meets a long stderr. withTimeoutOrNull , never withTimeout . The repo-wide resultLauncher catches Throwable , which includes CancellationException — a withTimeout here would be swallowed and re-reported as an ordinary failure, hiding real cancellation. destroyForcibly in finally , plus a live-child registry and a shutdown hook, so closing the window leaves no orphaned adb processes. spawnDetached is deliberately not registered with that hook. Booting an emulator starts the user's process, not ours; quitting Rectify must not kill their emulator. Finding the tools ToolResolver probes in a fixed order: the path the user chose, $ANDROID_HOME , $ANDROID_SDK_ROOT , ~/Library/Android/sdk , /opt/homebrew/bin , /usr/local/bin , then PATH . title: Design system
text: Design system Two modules: presentation-core-styling holds the tokens, presentation-core-ui holds the components built from them. This documentation site is themed from the same values — see the note at the end . Tokens Theme exposes grouped token sets, reached as Theme.color.ink , Theme.spacing.spacingL , Theme.typography.body and so on. Nothing in the UI hardcodes a colour or a size. Colour Authored in OKLCH and converted to sRGB at build time, with the original triplet kept in a trailing comment for traceability. Group Light Dark bg #F6F6F5 #1E1E20 chrome #EDEDEB #262628 stage #E7E7E4 #151517 surface #FFFFFF #2B2B2E ink / ink2 / ink3 #1A1A1C / #5B5B61 / #8B8B91 #F1F1F2 / #A3A3AA / #707077 focus #007DF2 #53A0FF Lines and fills are alpha over the surface , not opaque greys: line is rgba(0,0,0,.08) , line2 .14 , hover .045 , seg .06 , codeBg .035 . That is why they read correctly on surface and on stage without a second set of tokens. The signal colours are identical in both themes by design: Token Value Means annotate #F13936 An annotation rectangle sentFixed #3EAB5E Sent, or verified fixed warnStillOff #E69825 Working, or still off measure #007DF2 Measure mode Type Roboto Flex for everything a person reads; JetBrains Mono for everything a machine reports — versions, resolutions, fps, ids, file names, key hints. The mono roles carry the tnum feature so digits keep a fixed advance and live values stop jittering as they update. title: Build and testing
text: Build and testing One target Every module applies kotlin("jvm") . There is no Kotlin Multiplatform plugin, no platform targets, no expect / actual , and sources sit in the classic src/main/kotlin and src/test/kotlin . Compose Multiplatform is still used — for the renderer and the component library, not for multiplatform reach. Adding a platform is a migration back to KMP, not a flag: re-add the plugin in the convention plugins, split src/main into commonMain plus a platform source set, and add a runnable module for the new platform. Convention plugins Four, in build-logic/convention , all extending BaseConventionPlugin — a template method over three hooks, run in a fixed order: configurePlugin → configureJvm → configureDependencies . application feature library di kotlin("jvm") + java-library ✓ ✓ ✓ — Compose plugins ✓ ✓ — — Compose dependencies ✓ ✓ — — jvmToolchain(21) + explicitApi() ✓ ✓ ✓ — compose.desktop.currentOs ✓ — — — kotlin-test on test — ✓ ✓ — Koin — — — ✓ java-library is applied explicitly because kotlin("jvm") alone does not guarantee the api configuration, and several modules use api(projects.x) . compose.desktop.currentOs — the Skiko renderer — is only on the application plugin. Only the module that actually opens a window needs it. Three modules skip convention plugins entirely: desktop-application , mcp-application and docs-generator . Each is a binary with its own deliberately minimal classpath, not a library in the app's dependency graph. This is documented rather than accidental — do not "fix" it by inventing a fift
